newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks eye upside with help of pension funds.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks eye upside with help of pension funds.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are set to tackle the 20,000 point barrier, but may first pause for breath after a healthy eight percent rise in April inspired by pension fund buying, market sources say.

"In the very near term a correction may occur but pension funds should keep buying and inspire other market participants," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities. "So any weak spell will probably be short-lived, if there is one at all.
"The next goal for the Nikkei average is 20,000," he said.
Trust banks, which manage pension fund money, were large net buyers of Japanese stocks in April, the latest Tokyo Stock Exchange data showed.

Net trust bank purchases totalled 355.38 billion yen ($2.79 billion) on the Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya bourses in the four-week period from March 31 through April 25. The bulk of that buying is thought to have been on behalf of pension funds.

Those purchases eclipsed net buying by foreign investors, which totalled 155.28 billion yen ($1.22 billion) during the same period. Foreigners were net sellers of Japanese stocks in the third week of April for the first time in 11 weeks.

Brokers said Wall Street's rally and a gradual shift into stocks from bonds on the back of ultra-low domestic interest rates have also been supportive factors in recent weeks. But fund managers at major life insurers say their purchases have also contributed greatly to supporting the Nikkei average.

"The money is doled out and then index-linked buying emerges to send the Nikkei average higher, regardless of whether there are reasons to buy or not," Noboru Yorita, general manager at Tachibana Securities Co Ltd, said.
"Once buying starts, sellers become afraid of being left behind and dealers jump on the bandwagon to provide more support," he added.
The buying spree even managed to cushion the impact on the stock market of Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co's recent failure.
Nissan became the first insurer to fail in the post-war period when it was ordered by the Finance Ministry late last month to start shutting down its business.
Nissan Life buckled under excessive liabilities stemming from the bursting of Japan's real estate and stock price bubble in the late 1980s.

Life insurers are not listed in Japan, but shares of firms such as Nissan Fire & Marine Insurance Co Ltd and Hitachi Ltd, in which Nissan Life is a major shareholder, sagged momentarily, as investors feared that the shares would be dumped onto the stock market.

"The government is afraid the frail stock market will be battered should more insurers fail, following Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co," Akagiya Security Co Ltd managing director Shinji Mitsumori said. "Pension fund buying is just a form of price-keeping operation conducted by the government."

Rumours of allocations by the Postal Life Insurance Bureau (Kampo), the largest institutional investor in Japan, have also helped keep share prices aloft. Kampo had total assets of 97.22 trillion yen ($765 billion) at the end of February.
Inflows of pension fund money, which are expected to last until June, have put worries over a possible meltdown in Japan's financial system on the backburner.
Market sources also believe the Nikkei average is establishing a floor around 19,000, nearly 1,000 points above its levels at the end of the fiscal year in March.

"The problems with financial institutions still have to be cleaned up, although the most troubled bank, Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, has embarked on a rehabilitation," Ken Ishikida, Sanyo Securities general manager, said. "But for the time being, the market is concentrating on testing the upper side of the indices." ($1=127 yen)
